stem: A relation R on the set {1, 2, 3} is defined as R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)}. Which of the following correctly describes R?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Checking only reflexivity and missing that (a,b) and (b,a) pairs are both present (vacuously or by identity) and that transitivity holds via all (a,a) pairs.
Checking only symmetry and missing reflexivity; the identity relation is symmetric (each (a,a) is its own symmetric pair) but that alone misses the full picture.

The identity relation {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)} satisfies all three: reflexive because every element pairs with itself; symmetric because (a,a) reversed is (a,a); transitive because whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in R we have a=b=c so (a,c)=(a,a) is in R. This makes it an equivalence relation.
Checking only transitivity and missing that reflexive and symmetric also hold; applying only the transitivity check without verifying the other properties.

explanation: The identity relation on any non-empty set is always an equivalence relation, satisfying all three defining properties simultaneously.

explanation_sections.punchline: The identity relation is the smallest equivalence relation on any set, holding all three properties by construction.
explanation_sections.approach: State the property and contrast the confusable one. For reflexive: every element must pair with itself; check (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) all present. For symmetric: if (a,b) is in R then (b,a) must be in R; here every pair (a,a) is its own symmetric partner. For transitive: if (a,b) and (b,c) in R then (a,c) must be in R; only pairs (a,a) exist so a=b=c making (a,c)=(a,a) which is present. All three hold.
explanation_sections.lesson: An identity relation on a finite set always satisfies reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, making it an equivalence relation.
explanation_sections.timing: About 45 seconds. Read each property definition and test it against the three pairs directly. No calculation needed.
